# Part I · The memory problem left by n-grams {.section-slide}

## Start with the prediction problem

::: {.pause-panel .memory-pause}
**PAUSE · PREDICT THE MISSING WORD**

> The keys to the cabinet ___ on the table.

1. Which earlier word determines the answer?
2. What does a bigram model see when it reaches the blank?
:::

::: {.problem-instruction}
Keep the full sentence visible—but make the prediction using only the final available token.
:::

## The relevant word may be far behind

::: {.dependency-stage}
<span class="fragment cue-token">The <b>keys</b></span>
<span class="fragment intervening">to</span>
<span class="fragment intervening">the</span>
<span class="fragment local-history">cabinet</span>
<span class="fragment prediction-slot">___</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .dependency-arc}
<div class="arc-line"></div><span>plural agreement must survive four positions</span>
:::

:::: {.memory-comparison}
::: {.fragment .memory-card .sentence-evidence}
<small>THE SENTENCE CONTAINS</small>

`keys → plural → are`
:::
::: {.fragment .memory-card .bigram-evidence}
<small>THE BIGRAM RETAINS</small>

`cabinet → ?`
:::
::::

<div class="citation">Long-distance agreement illustrates the fixed-context limitation of n-gram models [@jurafsky2026slp, Chs. 3 and 9].</div>

## Inspect exactly where the information disappears

::: {.context-window-demo}
<div class="sentence-track"><span class="lost-cue">keys</span><span>to</span><span>the</span><span class="active-history">cabinet</span><b>?</b></div>
<div class="window-bracket"><i></i><strong>BIGRAM INPUT</strong><i></i></div>
:::

:::: {.information-ledger}
::: {.fragment .ledger-row .available-row}
<b>Needed feature</b><span>subject number = plural</span><strong>available earlier</strong>
:::
::: {.fragment .ledger-row .discarded-row}
<b>Model input</b><span>previous token = cabinet</span><strong>plural cue discarded</strong>
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .danger}
Smoothing can repair a missing **count**. It cannot recover information that the model's history representation has already discarded.
:::

<div class="citation">N-gram smoothing and context-length limitations are distinct problems [@jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 3].</div>

## Why not simply increase n?

::: {.order-growth}
<div class="fragment"><small>BIGRAM</small><b>1 word</b><span>$|V|^2$ possible pairs</span></div>
<i class="fragment">→</i>
<div class="fragment"><small>5-GRAM</small><b>4 words</b><span>$|V|^5$ possible sequences</span></div>
<i class="fragment">→</i>
<div class="fragment growth-warning"><small>LONG DEPENDENCY</small><b>unknown length</b><span>no fixed n is enough</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .growth-calculation}
With $|V|=50{,}000$, a 5-gram table permits $(50{,}000)^5\approx\mathbf{3.1\times10^{23}}$ distinct sequences.
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Increasing $n$ buys a longer window, not a mechanism for deciding which earlier information matters.
:::

<div class="citation">Higher-order n-gram parameter growth and sparsity: [@jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 3].</div>

## One n-gram model, two different failures

:::: {.failure-fork}
::: {.failure-case .sparsity-case}
<small>FAILURE 1 · GENERALIZATION</small>

**“the cat rested”** was seen  
**“the dog rested”** was not

$$
\text{count(the dog rested)}=0
$$

<b>Bengio’s repair</b>

Learn that *cat* and *dog* can behave similarly.
:::
::: {.fragment .failure-case .memory-case}
<small>FAILURE 2 · MEMORY</small>

**keys** to the cabinet **are**  
but the window sees only **cabinet**

$$
P(w_t\mid w_{t-n:t-1})
$$

<b>RNN’s repair</b>

Carry an evolving state beyond a fixed suffix.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
These are separate defects: **continuous representations** address sparse generalization; **recurrence** addresses how context is carried.
:::

<div class="citation">The window-based neural LM addresses the curse of dimensionality while retaining finite context [@bengio2003neural; @jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 9].</div>

## Bengio’s wager: nearby words should share evidence

::: {.bengio-example}
<div class="seen-context"><small>SEEN</small><span>the</span><b>cat</b><span>rested</span><strong>high evidence</strong></div>
<div class="embedding-neighborhood" aria-label="Cat and dog occupy nearby locations in an embedding plane, while cabinet is farther away.">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 520 320" role="img">
    <line x1="55" y1="270" x2="480" y2="270"></line><line x1="55" y1="270" x2="55" y2="35"></line>
    <circle class="neighbor-halo" cx="205" cy="145" r="75"></circle>
    <circle class="cat-point" cx="180" cy="130" r="18"></circle><text x="180" y="100">cat</text>
    <circle class="dog-point" cx="235" cy="165" r="18"></circle><text x="235" y="205">dog</text>
    <circle class="far-point" cx="410" cy="75" r="18"></circle><text x="410" y="113">cabinet</text>
    <text class="axis-label" x="390" y="302">learned dimension 1</text>
    <text class="axis-label" x="15" y="25">dimension 2</text>
  </svg>
</div>
<div class="unseen-context fragment"><small>UNSEEN</small><span>the</span><b>dog</b><span>rested</span><strong>borrow evidence</strong></div>
:::

$$
\mathbf e(\text{cat})\approx \mathbf e(\text{dog})
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P(\text{rested}\mid\text{the, cat})\approx P(\text{rested}\mid\text{the, dog})
$$

<div class="citation">Distributed word representations let a training sequence inform semantically neighboring sequences [@bengio2003neural].</div>

<div class="citation paper-full-citation">Original Figure 1 from Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent, and Christian Jauvin (2003), “A Neural Probabilistic Language Model,” <em>Journal of Machine Learning Research</em> 3: 1137–1155, p. 1142. <a href="https://jmlr.org/papers/v3/bengio03a.html">Paper and PDF</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
This is Bengio et al.'s window-based neural probabilistic language model, shown with the same concrete context from the previous slide.

- Begin at the left: each discrete word index selects a learned vector from a shared embedding table.
- Concatenate the vectors for the fixed context window into one vector, $\mathbf x=(C(w_{t-1}),C(w_{t-2}),\ldots,C(w_{t-n+1}))$.
- The hidden layer learns distributed features of that context: $\mathbf a=\tanh(\mathbf d+H\mathbf x)$.
- The output layer produces one unnormalized log-probability per vocabulary item: $\mathbf y=\mathbf b+W\mathbf x+U\mathbf a$; softmax normalizes these scores.
- In the original paper, the embedding parameters and probability network are learned jointly by maximizing the training-corpus log likelihood.
- The curved dashed route is the paper's optional direct connection $W\mathbf x$. When direct connections are disabled, $W=0$.
- Emphasize the limitation without developing it yet: this is still a fixed context window. We will decide in the next review how to use that boundary to motivate recurrence.
:::

## A fixed-window neural language model

:::: {.fixed-window-example}
::: {.fixed-window-equations}
<div class="equation-row output-equation">
<strong>output distribution</strong>

$$
\hat{\mathbf y}=\operatorname{softmax}(U\mathbf h+\mathbf b_2)
\in\mathbb R^{|V|}
$$
</div>

<div class="equation-row hidden-equation">
<strong>hidden layer</strong>

$$
\mathbf h=f(W\mathbf e+\mathbf b_1)
$$
</div>

<div class="equation-row embedding-equation">
<strong>concatenated word embeddings</strong>

$$
\mathbf e=[\mathbf e^{(1)};\mathbf e^{(2)};\mathbf e^{(3)};\mathbf e^{(4)}]
$$
</div>

<div class="equation-row input-equation">
<strong>words / one-hot vectors</strong>

$$
\mathbf x^{(1)},\mathbf x^{(2)},\mathbf x^{(3)},\mathbf x^{(4)}
$$
</div>
:::

::: {.fixed-window-architecture}
```{=html}

The words the, students, opened, and their map to four embedding groups, which are concatenated and transformed into a hidden layer. <div class="citation paper-full-citation">Reproduced from Diyi Yang, “Language Models and Recurrent Neural Networks,” <em>Stanford CS224N/Ling284</em>, Winter 2026, slide 23. <a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/slides_w26/cs224n-2026-lecture04-rnnlm.pdf#page=21">Lecture slides</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Read the example from bottom to top.
- The fixed context is exactly four words: “the students opened their.” Each word begins as a one-hot vector $\mathbf x^{(i)}$.
- A shared embedding table maps each one-hot vector to $\mathbf e^{(i)}$, but the four embeddings are then concatenated into one position-specific vector $\mathbf e$.
- The matrix $W$ maps that concatenated vector to a hidden representation $\mathbf h$.
- The matrix $U$ maps the hidden representation to one score for every vocabulary item; softmax produces $\hat{\mathbf y}$.
- Point to “books” and “laptops” as plausible continuations. “A zoo” indicates that the output covers the full vocabulary, including implausible candidates with low probability.
- Transition question for the next review: what happens if the useful word lies before this four-word window, or if we want five, fifty, or five hundred input words?
:::

## Why the fixed window cannot scale

:::: {.window-limit-layout}
::: {.window-limit-story}
::: {.window-improvements}
<strong>IMPROVEMENTS OVER AN N-GRAM LM</strong>

<span>✓ No sparsity problem</span>
<span>✓ No table of all observed n-grams</span>
:::

::: {.fragment .window-problem .small-window-problem data-fragment-index="0"}
<b>1</b><p>The fixed window is <strong>too small</strong>.</p>
:::

::: {.fragment .window-problem .growing-w-problem data-fragment-index="1"}
<b>2</b><p>Enlarging the window enlarges <strong>$W$</strong>.</p>

$$
W\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times kd_e}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|W|=k\,d_h d_e
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .window-problem .finite-window-problem data-fragment-index="2"}
<b>3</b><p>No finite window can always be large enough.</p>
:::

::: {.fragment .window-problem .symmetry-problem data-fragment-index="3"}
<b>4</b><p>$\mathbf x^{(1)}$ and $\mathbf x^{(2)}$ use different blocks of $W$: <strong>no position symmetry</strong>.</p>
:::
:::

::::

::: {.fragment .any-length-need data-fragment-index="4"}
We need one neural architecture that can process **any-length input** without enlarging its parameter matrices.
:::

<div class="citation paper-full-citation">Adapted from Diyi Yang, “Language Models and Recurrent Neural Networks,” <em>Stanford CS224N/Ling284</em>, Winter 2026, slide 24. <a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/slides_w26/cs224n-2026-lecture04-rnnlm.pdf#page=22">Lecture slides</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Begin with the two improvements over an n-gram model: learned representations remove the exact-count sparsity problem, and the model does not store a table of observed n-grams.
- Reveal problem 1: the four-word window discards “proctor,” even if that word is useful for predicting “exams.”
- Reveal problem 2 and the lower expanded vector together. If the context contains $k$ embeddings of dimension $d_e$, the concatenated vector has dimension $kd_e$. Therefore $W$ has shape $d_h\times kd_e$ and gains $d_h d_e$ parameters for every new position.
- Reveal problem 3: choosing a larger $k$ delays the boundary but never removes it.
- Reveal problem 4: concatenation assigns a separate block of $W$ to each position. The same word is processed differently in position 1 and position 2; the architecture has no symmetry across time.
- Final reveal: ask for an architecture whose parameter count is independent of sequence length and whose same transformation can be reused at every position. This is the opening for recurrence; do not show the RNN equation yet.
:::

::: {.shared-w-idea}
**CORE IDEA** · Apply the same weights $W$ **repeatedly**.
:::

<div class="citation paper-full-citation">Adapted from Diyi Yang, “Language Models and Recurrent Neural Networks,” <em>Stanford CS224N/Ling284</em>, Winter 2026, slide 25. <a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/slides_w26/cs224n-2026-lecture04-rnnlm.pdf#page=23">Lecture slides</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Start with one input, one hidden state, and an optional output.
- Reveal successive time steps. At every reveal, point to the label $W$ on the horizontal connection.
- The important change from the fixed-window model is not merely that there are more boxes. It is that every time step uses the same transformation rather than receiving its own position-specific block of a growing matrix.
- The ellipsis means the sequence can continue without adding a new parameter matrix.
- Inputs, hidden states, and outputs may have different dimensions; weight sharing means the relevant matrices are reused at every time step.
- End on the core idea. Do not introduce the state-update equation until the next slide.
:::

At every position: **read one input → update the state with the same $W$ → pass the state forward**.

<div class="citation paper-full-citation">Clause and output candidates adapted from Diyi Yang, “Language Models and Recurrent Neural Networks,” <em>Stanford CS224N/Ling284</em>, Winter 2026, slides 23–26. <a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/slides_w26/cs224n-2026-lecture04-rnnlm.pdf#page=24">Lecture slides</a>.</div>

- Reveal the clause one word at a time. Each new word creates one more application of the same computation.
- At “the,” there is only the first input and first hidden state.
- Reveal “students,” then point to the horizontal $W$: the previous state is carried into the next computation.
- Repeat for “opened” and “their.” The graph grows in time, but its parameters do not; every horizontal edge uses the same $W$.
- On the last reveal, map $h^{(4)}$ through $U$ and show the next-word distribution. “Books” receives the largest illustrated probability, while “laptops” remains plausible.
- Explain the terminology: this wide diagram is the RNN **unfolded through time**. The compact loop form folds these repeated copies back into one recurrent cell with shared parameters.
:::

## One recurrent cell, reused through time

:::: {.cell-math-layout}
::: {.cell-math-left}
```{=html}
<div class="single-cell-visual">
<svg viewBox="0 0 720 350" role="img" aria-label="One recurrent neural network cell. A magenta input x t enters through W x, a red previous state h t minus 1 enters through W h, the cell produces the next red state h t, and an optional green output y hat t leaves through U.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="cell-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z"></path></marker>
  </defs>

    <rect x="35" y="130" width="120" height="90" rx="15"></rect>

    <rect x="300" y="260" width="120" height="70" rx="14"></rect>

    <text x="360" y="343">x<tspan baseline-shift="sub">t</tspan></text>
  </g>

  <g class="rnn-cell-body">
    <rect x="275" y="105" width="170" height="120" rx="24"></rect>
    <text class="cell-title" x="360" y="158">RNN CELL</text>
    <text class="cell-operation" x="360" y="194">tanh</text>
  </g>

  <path class="cell-edge state-edge" d="M448 175 H565"></path>
  <g class="current-state">
    <rect x="565" y="130" width="120" height="90" rx="15"></rect>
    <circle cx="595" cy="175" r="11"></circle><circle cx="625" cy="175" r="11"></circle><circle cx="655" cy="175" r="11"></circle>
    <text x="625" y="115">h<tspan baseline-shift="sub">t</tspan></text>
  </g>

  <path class="cell-edge output-edge" d="M625 128 V92"></path><text class="cell-weight output-weight" x="670" y="113">U</text>
  <g class="current-output">

    <circle cx="595" cy="57" r="10"></circle><circle cx="625" cy="57" r="10"></circle><circle cx="655" cy="57" r="10"></circle>

  </g>

```

::: {.cell-equations}
::: {.state-equation}
<small>STATE UPDATE</small>

$$
\mathbf h_t=\tanh\!\left(W_h\mathbf h_{t-1}+W_x\mathbf x_t+\mathbf b_h\right)
$$
:::
::: {.output-equation-cell}
<small>OPTIONAL OUTPUT</small>

$$
\hat{\mathbf y}_t=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(U\mathbf h_t+\mathbf b_y\right)
$$
:::
:::
:::

::: {.cell-evaluation}
<div class="evaluation-heading advantage-heading">WHAT THIS BUYS US</div>

<div class="evaluation-point advantage-point"><b>1</b><p><strong>Any input length</strong><span>Repeat the cell for every arriving token.</span></p></div>
<div class="fragment evaluation-point advantage-point" data-fragment-index="0"><b>2</b><p><strong>Fixed parameter count</strong><span>$W_h$, $W_x$, and $U$ do not grow with sequence length.</span></p></div>
<div class="fragment evaluation-point advantage-point" data-fragment-index="1"><b>3</b><p><strong>History reaches the present</strong><span>$\mathbf h_t$ depends on $\mathbf h_{t-1}$.</span></p></div>
<div class="fragment evaluation-point advantage-point" data-fragment-index="2"><b>4</b><p><strong>Time-step symmetry</strong><span>The same matrices process every position.</span></p></div>

<div class="fragment evaluation-heading disadvantage-heading" data-fragment-index="3">WHAT IT COSTS US</div>

<div class="fragment evaluation-point disadvantage-point" data-fragment-index="3"><b>5</b><p><strong>Sequential computation</strong><span>$\mathbf h_t$ must wait for $\mathbf h_{t-1}$.</span></p></div>
<div class="fragment evaluation-point disadvantage-point" data-fragment-index="4"><b>6</b><p><strong>Fragile long-range learning</strong><span>Repeated updates can make signals fade or explode.</span></p></div>

::: {.fragment .cell-next-question data-fragment-index="5"}
Can one state preserve useful information through many repeated updates?
:::
:::
::::

<div class="citation paper-full-citation">RNN formulation and trade-offs adapted from Diyi Yang, “Language Models and Recurrent Neural Networks,” <em>Stanford CS224N/Ling284</em>, Winter 2026, slides 25–27. <a href="https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/slides_w26/cs224n-2026-lecture04-rnnlm.pdf#page=25">Lecture slides</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Read the diagram before the equations. The current input $\mathbf x_t$ and previous state $\mathbf h_{t-1}$ meet inside one recurrent cell.
- Match each arrow to a term in the state update: $W_x\mathbf x_t$, $W_h\mathbf h_{t-1}$, and the bias $\mathbf b_h$.
- The nonlinearity produces the updated state $\mathbf h_t$, which is both passed to the next time step and optionally mapped through $U$ to an output distribution.
- Reveal the advantages in order. Stress that arbitrary input length does not mean growing matrices; it means repeated application of the same matrices.
- Reveal the costs only after the benefits are established. Sequential computation is an architectural cost. Fragile long-range learning is a training problem that we have not explained yet.
- End with the question. It motivates inspecting repeated derivatives through the unfolded graph without prematurely teaching the vanishing-gradient derivation.
:::

      <rect x="300" y="415" width="125" height="74" rx="14"></rect>

::: {.bp-direction-cue}
Forward computation <span>→</span> · gradient flow <b>←</b>
:::
:::

::: {.single-cell-backprop-formulas}
::: {.bp-formula-card .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
<b>1 · OUTPUT ERROR</b>

$$
\boldsymbol\delta_z=\hat{\mathbf y}_t-\mathbf y_t
$$
:::

::: {.bp-formula-card .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
<b>2 · REACH THE HIDDEN STATE</b>

$$
\mathbf g_h=U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_z
$$
:::

::: {.bp-formula-card .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
<b>3 · PASS THROUGH TANH</b>

$$
\boldsymbol\delta_a
=\mathbf g_h\odot(1-\mathbf h_t^2)
$$
:::

::: {.bp-formula-card .bp-parameter-card .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
<b>4 · FOLLOW BOTH INPUT BRANCHES</b>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{W_h}L_t&=\boldsymbol\delta_a\mathbf h_{t-1}^{\top},
&\nabla_{\mathbf h_{t-1}}L_t&=W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a\\
\nabla_{W_x}L_t&=\boldsymbol\delta_a\mathbf x_t^{\top},
&\nabla_{\mathbf b_h}L_t&=\boldsymbol\delta_a
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::
::::

<div class="citation">Local RNN backpropagation follows the computational graph from softmax cross-entropy through the hidden-state update [@jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 9].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Keep the complete forward cell visible, but reveal the backward path one stage at a time. Each numbered gradient overlay on the left is synchronized with the formula carrying the same number on the right.
- Stage 1: for softmax with cross-entropy, the derivative with respect to the logits is the prediction minus the one-hot target, $\boldsymbol\delta_z=\hat{\mathbf y}_t-\mathbf y_t$.
- Stage 2: multiply by $U^\top$ to move the error from output space into hidden-state space. For this first local derivation, $\mathbf g_h$ contains only the contribution from the output at time $t$.
- Stage 3: differentiate the tanh nonlinearity elementwise. Keep $\boldsymbol\delta_a$ visible; it is the reusable error signal for every branch entering the cell pre-activation.
- Stage 4: the same $\boldsymbol\delta_a$ produces gradients for $W_h$, $W_x$, and $\mathbf b_h$. The branch $W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a$ sends credit to the previous hidden state.
- End by pointing to $\nabla_{\mathbf h_{t-1}}L_t$. We have derived one local backward step; the next slide expands the objective from one output loss to all output losses in the sequence.
:::

## One prediction, one cross-entropy loss

:::: {.temporal-loss-layout}
::: {.temporal-loss-example}
<div class="loss-context"><span>the</span><span>students</span><span>opened</span><b>their</b></div>

<div class="loss-prediction">
<small>AT TIME $t$</small>

$$
\hat{\mathbf y}_t
=P_\theta(w_{t+1}\mid w_{1:t})
$$

<div class="target-probability"><span>target: <b>books</b></span><strong>$\hat y_{t,\text{books}}=0.62$</strong></div>
</div>

::: {.fragment .loss-result data-fragment-index="0"}
<small>CROSS-ENTROPY AT THIS OUTPUT</small>

$$
J^{(t)}(\theta)
=-\sum_{v\in V}y_{t,v}\log\hat y_{t,v}
=-\log 0.62
\approx 0.48
$$
:::
:::

::: {.temporal-loss-sequence}
<div class="loss-sequence-heading">ONE LOSS AT EVERY PREDICTED TOKEN</div>

<div class="time-loss-row fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>t = 1</b><span>the → students</span><strong>J<sup>(1)</sup>(θ)</strong></div>
<div class="time-loss-row fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>t = 2</b><span>students → opened</span><strong>J<sup>(2)</sup>(θ)</strong></div>
<div class="time-loss-row fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>t = 3</b><span>opened → their</span><strong>J<sup>(3)</sup>(θ)</strong></div>
<div class="time-loss-row active-time-loss fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>t = 4</b><span>their → books</span><strong>J<sup>(4)</sup>(θ)</strong></div>

::: {.fragment .sequence-objective data-fragment-index="2"}
$$
J(\theta)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}J^{(t)}(\theta)
$$
:::
:::
::::

::: {.pause-panel .bptt-pause .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
**PAUSE · THE PARAMETERS ARE SHARED THROUGH TIME**

How does the gradient from **every** $J^{(t)}(\theta)$ reach the same $W_h$, $W_x$, and $U$—and how should those contributions be combined before one update?
:::

<div class="citation">Token-level cross-entropy losses and their sum over a sequence follow the recurrent language-model objective [@jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 9].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Keep the concrete prediction visible: after “the students opened their,” the target is “books,” and the model assigns it probability $0.62$.
- Reveal the first calculation. Because the target is one-hot, the vocabulary-wide cross-entropy collapses to $-\log\hat y_{t,\text{books}}=-\log 0.62\approx0.48$.
- Reveal the four time-indexed losses together. Each output is supervised by the next observed word.
- Reveal the total sequence objective as the sum of those losses.
- End on the PAUSE panel. Do not answer it here. Ask students to identify two issues: multiple losses can influence one earlier state, and the same parameter matrices occur at every time step.
:::

## When two gradient paths meet, they add

:::: {.gradient-merge-layout}
::: {.gradient-merge-graph}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 760 600" role="img" aria-label="A hidden state h t sends information to the current output loss J t and to the next hidden state h t plus 1. During backpropagation, blue gradient paths from both downstream branches meet at h t and add.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="merge-forward-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#1a9a94"></path></marker>
    <marker id="merge-backward-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="#356fa8" fill-opacity=".68"></path></marker>
  </defs>

  <g class="merge-forward">
    <g class="merge-node merge-source"><rect x="275" y="245" width="210" height="120" rx="22"></rect><text class="merge-symbol" x="380" y="320">h<tspan baseline-shift="sub">t</tspan></text></g>
    <path d="M430 243 C475 175 535 145 600 145"></path>
    <path d="M488 305 H610"></path>
    <g class="merge-node merge-loss"><rect x="580" y="55" width="150" height="88" rx="17"></rect><text class="merge-symbol" x="655" y="112">J<tspan baseline-shift="super">(t)</tspan></text></g>
    <g class="merge-node merge-future"><rect x="610" y="255" width="120" height="100" rx="17"></rect><text x="670" y="292">NEXT STATE</text><text class="merge-symbol" x="670" y="330">h<tspan baseline-shift="sub">t+1</tspan></text></g>
  </g>

  <g class="fragment merge-backward merge-local" data-fragment-index="0">
    <path d="M580 115 C505 125 455 175 420 245"></path>
    <text x="490" y="155">local contribution</text>
  </g>
  <g class="fragment merge-backward merge-future-path" data-fragment-index="1">
    <path d="M607 330 H488"></path>
    <text x="550" y="390">future contribution</text>
  </g>
  <g class="fragment merge-sum-badge" data-fragment-index="2">
    <circle cx="470" cy="275" r="32"></circle>
    <text x="470" y="287">+</text>
  </g>

  <g class="fragment merge-update" data-fragment-index="3">
    <path d="M275 305 H115"></path>
    <g><rect x="25" y="250" width="145" height="110" rx="18"></rect><text x="97" y="291">TOTAL</text><text x="97" y="322">GRADIENT AT</text><text class="merge-symbol" x="97" y="350">h<tspan baseline-shift="sub">t</tspan></text></g>
  </g>
</svg>
```
:::

::: {.gradient-merge-solution}
<div class="merge-given"><small>THE FORWARD GRAPH BRANCHES</small><p>$\mathbf h_t$ influences the loss now and the recurrent state next.</p></div>

::: {.fragment .merge-contribution data-fragment-index="0"}
<b>PATH 1 · CURRENT OUTPUT</b>

$$
\left.\nabla_{\mathbf h_t}J\right|_{J^{(t)}}
=U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_z^{(t)}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .merge-contribution data-fragment-index="1"}
<b>PATH 2 · FUTURE STATE</b>

$$
\left.\nabla_{\mathbf h_t}J\right|_{\mathbf h_{t+1}}
=W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a^{(t+1)}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .merge-total data-fragment-index="2"}
<small>BACKPROPAGATION RULE AT A BRANCH</small>

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf h_t}J
=U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_z^{(t)}
+W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a^{(t+1)}
$$

<strong>Every downstream route contributes; the contributions add.</strong>
:::
:::
::::

<div class="citation">Gradient accumulation at a branching node is the multivariable chain rule applied to the unfolded recurrent computation graph [@goodfellow2016deep, Chs. 6 and 10; @jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 9].</div>

::: {.notes}
- This slide is the worked answer to the preceding PAUSE question at the level of one hidden state.
- Read the forward graph first. The state $\mathbf h_t$ has two downstream uses: it produces the current output and it enters the next recurrent state.
- Reveal the blue path from $J^{(t)}$. It contributes $U^\top\boldsymbol\delta_z^{(t)}$.
- Reveal the path returning from $\mathbf h_{t+1}$. It contributes $W_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_a^{(t+1)}$.
- Reveal the plus sign and total gradient. Backpropagation does not choose one route; it sums all downstream contributions at the shared node.
- This same principle will repeat at every hidden state when the RNN is unfolded through time.
:::

<div class="citation">Backpropagation through time is ordinary backpropagation applied to the RNN unfolded as a computation graph [@werbos1990backpropagation; @goodfellow2016deep, Ch. 10; @jurafsky2026slp, Ch. 9].</div>

::: {.notes}
- This slide is intentionally illustration-only. Let the spatial structure carry the explanation.
- First read the solid teal forward pass: each input updates a hidden state; every hidden state produces a token-level loss; $W_h$ is reused along the horizontal chain.
- Reveal the first translucent-blue layer: every loss sends a local gradient into its hidden state.
- Reveal the second layer: those gradients then travel backward through the recurrent chain, from later states toward earlier states.
- Reveal the curved paths into the parameter hub: because the same $W_h$, $W_x$, and $U$ were used repeatedly, every time step contributes to the gradients of the same parameter tensors.
- Final reveal: the curved paths collect every time-step contribution into the shared parameter gradient; sum them, then perform one optimizer update.
- End with the full backward chain visible. The unresolved question is now how repeated Jacobian products behave when credit must travel across many time steps.
:::

## Having fun with RNNs

::: {.recipe-generation-lead}
Train a character-level RNN on recipe text—then repeatedly sample its next character to invent a new “recipe” in the learned style.
:::

:::: {.rnn-recipe-layout}
::: {.generated-recipe-card}
<div class="recipe-machine-label">SAMPLED FROM THE MODEL</div>

<h3>CARAMEL CORN<br>GARLIC BEEF</h3>

<div class="recipe-rule"></div>

<div class="recipe-meta"><span><b>CATEGORIES</b> Savory, Desserts</span><span><b>YIELD</b> 4 confused servings</span></div>

<div class="recipe-section-label">INGREDIENTS</div>

- 2 tbsp Parmesan cheese, ground
- ¼ tsp ground cloves
- 1 tsp cayenne pepper
- 1 cup pineapple chunks
- ½ cup toasted pecans
- 2 tbsp cocoa powder
- 1 cup caramel sauce

<div class="recipe-section-label">DIRECTIONS</div>

1. Glaze the ribs with caramel sauce.
2. Fold in pineapple, pecans, and cocoa.
3. Bake until the model predicts `<END>`.

<div class="recipe-warning">⚠ Structurally convincing does not mean edible—or safe.</div>
:::

Fictional sample inspired by the generated titles in <a href="https://gist.github.com/nylki/1efbaa36635956d35bcc">“do androids dream of cooking?”</a>; original preview image generated for this lecture.</div>

::: {.notes}
- This is a preview of the coding project: train a small character-level RNN on a corpus whose repeated structure is easy to recognize, then generate by feeding each sampled character back as the next input.
- Read the recipe card aloud. It is a compact fictional sample based on the style of the linked outputs. The model has learned recognizable surface conventions—an uppercase title, metadata, quantities, ingredients, and imperative cooking directions—even though the content is incoherent.
- The photograph is intentionally plausible but depicts the absurd combination suggested by the sampled recipe. It is an original lecture asset, not an image from the linked gist.
- Stress the warning: language-model fluency is not factuality, physical consistency, or safety. Students should treat outputs as text-generation artifacts, not cooking advice.
- Use the link as the project seed: students can inspect the historical char-RNN samples, then build a modern, small-scale version with transparent training and sampling code.
:::

:::: {.gradient-flow-question-layout}
::: {.gradient-product-rule .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
<small>FOUR STEPS BACK</small>

<div class="gradient-product-equation"><b>g₀ = A₁ᵀ A₂ᵀ A₃ᵀ A₄ᵀ g₄</b><span>Aₜ = ∂hₜ / ∂hₜ₋₁</span></div>

<span>The signal is multiplied again at every recurrent step.</span>
:::

::: {.pause-panel .gradient-flow-pause .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
**PAUSE · FOLLOW ONE SCALAR GRADIENT**

Given $g_4=1$ and the same local multiplier $a$ at four steps, compute

$$g_0=a^4g_4$$

for **$a=0.6$** and **$a=1.5$**. What changes as the dependency becomes longer?
:::
::::

<div class="citation">Long-range RNN gradients contain products of repeated recurrent Jacobians [@bengio1994learning; @pascanu2013difficulty; @goodfellow2016deep, Ch. 10].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Start with the same visual grammar as the BPTT slide: solid teal is the forward recurrent computation; translucent blue is the backward gradient.
- Reveal the loss-to-state gradient, then reveal its four backward recurrent steps.
- Each $A_t$ is the local Jacobian of one recurrent update. The gradient arriving at $h_0$ contains their product.
- Reveal the product only after students have followed the arrows visually.
- End on the PAUSE calculation. Do not give the two numerical answers on this slide.
:::

::: {.instability-synthesis .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
The problem is not “recurrence” alone. It is the **product of many local transformations**: repeated contraction forgets; repeated expansion destabilizes.
:::

<div class="citation">Vanishing and exploding gradients in recurrent networks are analyzed through products of Jacobians and their spectral behavior [@bengio1994learning; @pascanu2013difficulty].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Return to the two scalar cases from the PAUSE slide.
- Read the upper chain from right to left: $1$, $0.6$, $0.36$, $0.216$, $0.1296$. The translucent arrows deliberately fade with the gradient.
- Read the lower chain: $1$, $1.5$, $2.25$, $3.375$, $5.0625$. The orange arrows become more opaque and thicker as the signal grows.
- Reveal the consequences. A vanishing gradient prevents distant evidence from teaching early recurrent states. An exploding gradient produces unstable parameter updates and can create numerical overflow.
- Reveal the synthesis last. The scalar example is an intuition pump; in the vector RNN, matrix Jacobians contract or expand different directions at different rates.
- End with a forward-looking question for the next review: can the architecture create a path along which useful information and gradients travel with less repeated distortion?
:::

## A practical guardrail: gradient clipping

::::: {.gradient-clipping-layout}
::: {.gradient-clipping-story}
<div class="clipping-story-heading">WHEN THE GRADIENT EXPLODES</div>

<div class="clipping-step fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<b>1</b><p><strong>Measure the full gradient</strong><span>After BPTT, compute its global norm.</span></p>
</div>

<div class="clipping-norm fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<div class="gradient-vector long-gradient"><i></i><strong>‖g‖₂ = 18.0</strong></div>
<div class="threshold-line"><span>maximum allowed norm</span><b>τ = 5.0</b></div>
</div>

<div class="clipping-step fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
<b>2</b><p><strong>Too large? Rescale it</strong><span>Keep the direction; reduce only the magnitude.</span></p>
</div>

<div class="clipping-norm fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
<div class="gradient-vector clipped-gradient"><i></i><strong>‖g̃‖₂ = 5.0</strong></div>
<div class="direction-preserved">same update direction · safer step length</div>
</div>

<div class="clipping-step fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
<b>3</b><p><strong>Apply the optimizer update</strong><span>Use g̃ instead of the unstable g.</span></p>
</div>
:::

:::: {.gradient-clipping-algorithm}
<div class="algorithm-label">ALGORITHM · CLIP BY GLOBAL NORM</div>

<pre><code>input: gradient g, threshold τ

r ← ‖g‖₂

if r > τ:
    g̃ ← (τ / r) g
else:
    g̃ ← g

θ ← θ − η g̃</code></pre>

<div class="algorithm-invariant fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
<div class="algorithm-formula">g̃ = min(1, τ / ‖g‖₂) g</div>
<span>Norm capped at τ; direction preserved.</span>
</div>
::::
:::::

:::: {.clipping-limit-bridge .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
::: {.clipping-fixes}
<small>WHAT CLIPPING FIXES</small>

**Exploding gradients**  
Prevents one enormous update from destabilizing training.
:::
::: {.clipping-does-not-fix}
<small>WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX</small>

**Vanishing gradients**  
It cannot restore distant credit that has already faded.
:::
::: {.gated-opening}
Can the recurrent cell create a **protected memory path** instead of repeatedly rewriting everything?
:::
::::

<div class="citation">Global-norm clipping is a practical treatment for exploding gradients, but it does not solve long-term credit assignment [@pascanu2013difficulty; @goodfellow2016deep, Ch. 10].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Reveal the slide as a practical intervention, not as a new recurrent architecture.
- Stage 1: after BPTT has accumulated the complete gradient, compute its global Euclidean norm. In the visible example, the norm is $18$, above the threshold $\tau=5$.
- Stage 2: multiply the whole gradient vector by $5/18$. The new norm is exactly $5$, but every component is scaled by the same positive factor, so the update direction is preserved.
- Match the visual shortening on the left to the formula and pseudocode on the right.
- Stage 3: pass the clipped gradient to the optimizer. Clipping changes the step magnitude only when the norm exceeds the threshold.
- Reveal the final comparison. Clipping is highly useful for explosions, but it does not make a tiny long-range gradient large again.
- End on the question about a protected memory path. This creates the need for gated recurrent cells without introducing their equations yet.
:::

- “2012–2018” is a useful label for the gated-RNN heyday, not the invention period. LSTM dates to 1997 and GRU to 2014.
- The Transformer arrived in 2017; the transition was gradual and task-dependent, not an overnight replacement.
- Keep this overview at the flow level only. LSTM separates memory c from the visible hidden state h. GRU combines them into one state.
- These are clean redraws of the classical mechanisms so students will recognize the standard paper diagrams later.

<div class="gated-equation-sequence">
<div class="gate-equation-card fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><b>1 · RETAIN OR FORGET</b><span>forget gate</span><div>fₜ = σ(W_f [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_f)</div></div>
<div class="gate-equation-card fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>2 · PREPARE A WRITE</b><span>input gate + candidate</span><div>iₜ = σ(W_i [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_i)</div><div>gₜ = tanh(W_g [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_g)</div></div>
<div class="gate-equation-card memory-update-card fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>3 · UPDATE MEMORY</b><div>cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ gₜ</div></div>
<div class="gate-equation-card fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><b>4 · EXPOSE PART OF IT</b><span>output gate</span><div>oₜ = σ(W_o [hₜ₋₁; xₜ] + b_o)</div><div>hₜ = oₜ ⊙ tanh(cₜ)</div></div>
<div class="gate-shallow-takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><b>KEY PATH</b><span>cₜ uses an additive update that can preserve memory and gradient flow.</span></div>

</div>
::::

<div class="citation">Pedagogical redraw of the LSTM gated memory mechanism [@hochreiter1997lstm; @goodfellow2016deep, Ch. 10].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Reveal the forget path, then the write path, then the exposed hidden state. Match each colored overlay to the equation card with the same reveal.
- Keep the discussion shallow; the coding project will handle dimensions and implementation.
- The main conceptual difference is the additive cell-state update. LSTM does not guarantee perfect memory, but it creates a less distorted route.
:::

::::

::: {.nmt-transformer-seed .fragment data-fragment-index="7"}
The task is simple to state—but difficult to model: <b>how can a system preserve an entire source sentence while generating a new one?</b>
:::

<div class="citation">Google described its large-scale Neural Machine Translation system in 2016 [@wu2016gnmt]. This sequence-to-sequence problem later became the original proving ground for the Transformer [@vaswani2017attention].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Begin with the acronym: MT means Machine Translation. Define the task before introducing any architecture.
- Reveal the concrete French–English pair. The output is not a word-for-word substitution: it must preserve meaning and produce a fluent target sentence.
- Reveal the headline, then one modern use at a time. Do not read all four uses as a list; let each new setting broaden the same task.
- When the 2016 milestone appears, it covers and retires the example. This is not the invention of NMT: it marks Google's highly visible production-scale deployment of GNMT.
- Reveal the final question last. It creates the need for the encoder–decoder architecture on the next slide.
:::

## One recurrent chain: read, then write

::: {.seq2seq-lead}
The encoder's <b>final hidden state</b> becomes the decoder's <b>initial hidden state</b>.
:::

::: {.seq2seq-stage}

::: {.seq2seq-takeaway .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
The whole source sentence must pass through <b>one fixed-size vector, c</b>.
:::

<div class="citation">The sequence-to-sequence encoder–decoder maps a variable-length source to a variable-length target through a fixed-dimensional state [@sutskever2014sequence; @cho2014gru].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Reveal only the blue encoder region first. Follow the French tokens and point out that its state is updated after every input.
- Reveal the bridge second. The final encoder state h4 is renamed context c and used to initialize the decoder.
- Reveal the coral decoder region third. It continues recurrent computation, but now produces the English sequence token by token.
- “One RNN reads; another writes” describes two recurrent roles. The visual is one continuous recurrent chain joined by c; implementations may use separate encoder and decoder parameters.
- Reveal the fixed-size-vector statement last. This is the limitation that will make attention necessary.
:::

## Beyond translation: the encoder–decoder pattern

::: {.conditional-generalization}
<div><small>ENCODER</small><b>Represent an input x</b></div><span>→</span><div><small>DECODER</small><b>Generate an output y</b></div>
:::

::: {.conditional-task-stage}
<div class="conditional-task-card fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="0"><div class="task-number">1</div><div class="task-name"><small>SUMMARIZATION</small><b>Compress while preserving the central information</b></div><div class="task-io source-io"><small>DOCUMENT · x</small><span>The city approved a new nighttime bus service after a six-month trial showed increased demand…</span></div><div class="task-arrow">→</div><div class="task-io target-io"><small>SUMMARY · y</small><strong>City approves nighttime buses after successful trial.</strong></div><div class="task-paper"><a href="https://aclanthology.org/D15-1044/">Rush et al. · Abstractive Sentence Summarization (2015)</a></div></div>

<div class="conditional-task-card fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="1"><div class="task-number">2</div><div class="task-name"><small>DIALOGUE</small><b>Continue a conversation appropriately</b></div><div class="task-io source-io"><small>CONVERSATION · x</small><span>USER: My package has not arrived.<br>AGENT: Let me check the order.</span></div><div class="task-arrow">→</div><div class="task-io target-io"><small>NEXT RESPONSE · y</small><strong>Could you share your order number?</strong></div><div class="task-paper"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.05869">Vinyals &amp; Le · A Neural Conversational Model (2015)</a></div></div>

<div class="conditional-task-card fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="2"><div class="task-number">3</div><div class="task-name"><small>PARSING · AS SEQUENCE GENERATION</small><b>Linearize linguistic structure, then generate it</b></div><div class="task-io source-io"><small>SENTENCE · x</small><span>The package arrived.</span></div><div class="task-arrow">→</div><div class="task-io target-io tree-output"><small>LINEARIZED TREE · y</small><strong>(S (NP The package) (VP arrived))</strong></div><div class="task-paper"><a href="https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5635-grammar-as-a-foreign-language">Vinyals et al. · Grammar as a Foreign Language (2015)</a></div></div>

<div class="conditional-task-card fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="3"><div class="task-number">4</div><div class="task-name"><small>CODE GENERATION</small><b>Translate an intent into an executable sequence</b></div><div class="task-io source-io"><small>SPECIFICATION · x</small><span>Return the longest word in a list.</span></div><div class="task-arrow">→</div><div class="task-io target-io code-output"><small>PROGRAM · y</small><strong>max(words, key=len)</strong></div><div class="task-paper"><a href="https://aclanthology.org/P17-1041/">Yin &amp; Neubig · General-Purpose Code Generation (2017)</a></div></div>

<div class="conditional-task-synthesis fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><div class="task-chip">document <b>→</b> summary</div><div class="task-chip">dialogue <b>→</b> response</div><div class="task-chip">sentence <b>→</b> tree</div><div class="task-chip">specification <b>→</b> code</div></div>
:::

::: {.conditional-lm-definition .fragment data-fragment-index="4"}
<div class="conditional-lm-title"><small>ONE NAME FOR THE PATTERN</small><b>Conditional language model</b></div><div class="conditional-lm-equation">P(y | x) = ∏<sub>t=1</sub><sup>T</sup> P(y<sub>t</sub> | y<sub>&lt;t</sub>, x)</div><div class="conditional-lm-why"><b>LANGUAGE MODEL</b><span>generates y token by token</span><b>CONDITIONAL</b><span>every prediction also depends on x</span></div>
:::

<div class="citation">Representative early encoder–decoder applications include summarization, dialogue, linearized parsing, and code generation [@rush2015summarization; @vinyals2015conversation; @vinyals2015grammar; @yin2017code].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Start from the abstract pattern. Translation used source language x and target language y, but the architecture only requires an input and a generated output.
- Reveal one task card at a time; each replaces the previous card so students inspect one mapping rather than scan four boxes.
- For parsing, state the qualification explicitly: parsing becomes conditional sequence generation when the tree is linearized into tokens. Not every parser is a language model.
- After code generation, replace the example with four compact mappings. The changing task is defined by what x and y mean.
- Reveal the name and factorization with the synthesis. It is a language model because y is generated autoregressively. It is conditional because x remains an argument of every next-token distribution.
:::

## Training seq2seq: loss there, credit everywhere

::: {.seq2seq-training-lead}
The targets supervise the <b>decoder outputs</b>—then backpropagation trains the <b>entire encoder–decoder chain</b>.
:::

::: {.seq2seq-training-stage}

:::: {.seq2seq-training-synthesis .fragment data-fragment-index="4"}
::: {.training-where-loss}
<small>WHERE IS LOSS COMPUTED?</small><b>Only where target tokens are predicted.</b>
:::
::: {.training-what-updates}
<small>WHAT GETS UPDATED?</small><b>Decoder parameters, context path, and encoder parameters.</b>
:::
::::

<div class="citation">Sequence-to-sequence models are trained end-to-end with target-side token losses and gradients propagated through the full computation graph [@sutskever2014sequence; @goodfellow2016deep, Ch. 10].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Reveal the forward computation first. The encoder reads source tokens; the context initializes the decoder; the decoder predicts target tokens.
- Reveal the four decoder losses. Each prediction is compared with its gold target token using cross-entropy. No separate loss is attached to the encoder states.
- Sum the token losses into one sequence objective.
- Reveal the translucent backward path. Although supervision appears on the decoder side, the chain rule carries credit through every decoder state, through c, and back into every encoder state.
- End with the two-answer synthesis: loss location and parameter-update reach are different questions.
:::

## One vector must remember everything

::: {.nmt-bottleneck-stage}

  <g class="bottleneck-state decoder-bottleneck-state"><rect x="755" y="175" width="90" height="90" rx="16"></rect><text x="800" y="230">s₁</text></g><g class="bottleneck-state decoder-bottleneck-state"><rect x="890" y="175" width="90" height="90" rx="16"></rect><text x="935" y="230">s₂</text></g><g class="bottleneck-state decoder-bottleneck-state"><rect x="1025" y="175" width="90" height="90" rx="16"></rect><text x="1070" y="230">s₃</text></g><g class="bottleneck-state decoder-bottleneck-state"><rect x="1160" y="175" width="90" height="90" rx="16"></rect><text x="1205" y="230">s₄</text></g>

::: {.bottleneck-question .fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}
<small>PAUSE · FIND THE LIMITATION</small>
<b>What happens when the source is long, information-rich, or difficult to compress into one vector?</b>
:::

::: {.bottleneck-answer .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
<div class="bottleneck-limit"><small>THE BOTTLENECK</small><b>The decoder can consult only c—even when it needs one specific source detail.</b></div>
<div class="bottleneck-next"><span>COMING NEXT WEEK</span><strong>ATTENTION</strong><i>Can the decoder recover what it needs without forcing everything through one fixed-size memory?</i></div>
:::

<div class="citation">The fixed-length context vector was a central limitation of early encoder–decoder translation models; attention was introduced to address it [@bahdanau2015align].</div>

::: {.notes}
- Reuse the familiar translation graph; students should spend no effort decoding a new visual grammar.
- Reveal the translucent compression curves and pause. Ask what information the decoder can access after the encoder has finished.
- Let students name the fixed-context bottleneck before revealing the answer.
- Reveal only the word attention and the motivating question. Do not explain alignment scores, weights, or context sums in this lecture.
- Leave the final question visible as the bridge into next week.
:::
